ana_01.label: Dataset shape and funding normalization
ana_01.content: The dataset is 50 companies by 5 columns (Name, What It Does, Funding, Year Founded, Headquarters), with founding years spanning 2013 to 2025 — a tight 12-year window. Every funding string parses cleanly once normalized to millions of USD: '$60 B' becomes 60,000, '$182.6 B' becomes 182,600, '$830 M' becomes 830. Two companies record '$0 M' — Midjourney and Surge AI — which reflects famously bootstrapped or undisclosed financing rather than literally zero capital. There are no missing values in any column.

ana_02.label: Funding leaderboard and the power-law skew
ana_02.content: Cumulative funding is extraordinarily top-heavy. The 50 companies have raised about $305.7 B combined, but OpenAI ($182.6 B) and Anthropic ($60 B) alone account for $242.6 B — 79.4% of all capital on the list. Add Databricks ($20 B), Cursor ($3.3 B) and Mistral AI ($3.1 B) and the top five hold 88.0% of the total. The mean raise is $6,113 M but the median is just $735 M, an 8.3× gap that is the signature of a power-law distribution: a few giants and a long tail. This is a near-perfect picture of an AI gold rush where capital concentrates at the foundation-model frontier.

ana_03.label: Mean-median gap and the long tail
ana_03.content: The distribution is so skewed that summary statistics disagree wildly: the mean raise ($6,113 M) is 8.3× the median ($735 M). 32 of the 50 companies (64%) have raised under $1 B, and only 18 sit at or above $1 B. The two leaders carry the average single-handedly — OpenAI and Anthropic together are 79.4% of all capital, so the 'typical' AI 50 company looks nothing like the headline numbers. The list is really two lists stacked: a couple of generational outliers, and four dozen well-funded but ordinary-by-comparison startups.

ana_04.label: Country distribution — an American list
ana_04.content: The AI 50 is overwhelmingly American: 44 of 50 companies (88%) are headquartered in the United States. The international tail is just six companies across five countries — Sweden (Legora and Lovable, both Stockholm), plus one each in Canada (Cohere, Toronto), France (Mistral AI, Paris), Germany (Black Forest Labs, Freiburg) and the UK (Synthesia, London). No company on the list is headquartered in Asia. The private AI frontier, as Forbes frames it, is almost entirely a US story with a thin European edge.

ana_05.label: San Francisco's gravitational pull
ana_05.content: Zoom into the US and the concentration is even starker. Exactly half the entire list — 25 of 50 companies — is headquartered in the city of San Francisco. Another 8 sit elsewhere in California (Palo Alto ×3, Sunnyvale, San Mateo, San Jose, Los Angeles, Foster City), so 33 of 50 (66%) are Californian. Only 11 companies are in the rest of the US (mostly New York), and just 6 are international. One city holds as many AI-50 companies as the rest of the world and the rest of America combined. The Bay Area is not a hub; it is the center of gravity.

ana_06.label: The founding surge — born yesterday
ana_06.content: These are strikingly young companies. 34 of 50 (68%) were founded in 2020 or later, and 28 of 50 (56%) in 2022 or later — after the late-2022 ChatGPT moment that detonated the generative-AI boom. 2022 is the single biggest founding year with 11 companies, followed closely by 2023 with 10; together those two years alone produced 21 of the 50. The oldest company is Databricks (2013) and the newest is Thinking Machines Lab (2025), already valued enough to make the list within months of its founding. The AI 50 is less a hall of fame than a snapshot of a wave that crested in the last three years.

ana_07.label: What they actually do — the category map
ana_07.content: Sorting all 50 companies by what they build reveals a list dominated by applied AI, not just labs. The biggest category is generative media (8 companies: image, video, voice, music — ElevenLabs, Runway, Suno, Synthesia, Midjourney, Black Forest Labs, HeyGen, Krea), followed by foundation models (7) and AI infrastructure & chips (7, including Databricks, SambaNova, Together AI, Crusoe). Then come AI agents for customer-service/GTM/knowledge work (6), coding & app builders (5), robotics & autonomy (4), and clusters of three in healthcare, legal & finance, and data labeling. The long tail — search (Perplexity), productivity (Notion), security (Cyera), a voice tutor (Speak) — fills out the rest. Applied verticals outnumber the model labs roughly six to one.

ana_08.label: Where the money actually goes vs where the companies are
ana_08.content: Category counts and category capital tell opposite stories. Foundation models are only 7 of 50 companies (14%) but absorb $254.4 B — 83.2% of all funding on the list. Every other category combined — all the generative-media tools, agents, coding startups, robotics labs, healthcare and legal apps, and infrastructure — splits the remaining 16.8% ($51.3 B), and most of that 'everything else' is actually Databricks' $20 B sitting in infrastructure. So while the list is mostly applied AI by headcount, it is almost entirely a foundation-model story by dollars. The application layer is broad; the money is narrow.

ana_09.label: The vocabulary of the list — agents and generation
ana_09.content: The one-line descriptions themselves encode the 2025 zeitgeist. Five companies describe themselves around 'agents' (Cognition, Decagon, EliseAI, Glean, Sierra) — AI that acts, not just answers. Eight are built on generation/generative media (Black Forest Labs, ElevenLabs, Fal, HeyGen, Krea, Midjourney, Suno, Synthesia). Six describe coding, app-building or app-deployment (Baseten, Cognition, Cursor, Fireworks AI, Lovable, Replit). The recurring verbs — generate, build, automate, deploy — match Forbes' framing that the 2025 cohort moved from chatting to doing whole workflows.

ana_10.label: Age vs funding — youth is no barrier
ana_10.content: Older companies are not the best-funded ones; if anything the correlation between founding year and funding is slightly negative (Pearson r = -0.285). Broken into eras, the 2013-2018 cohort has a huge mean ($16,311 M) but that is entirely OpenAI and Databricks distorting it — its median is $850 M. The 2022-2025 cohort (28 companies) has a median of $668 M, not far below the older groups, despite being only a few years old. In this market, capital flows to perceived frontier potential, not to seniority: Thinking Machines Lab raised $2 B founded in 2025, while plenty of 2016-2018 companies sit under $1 B.

ana_11.label: Logo coverage — verified real vs wordmark
ana_11.content: Of the ~30 cached Wikimedia logos, manual verification against each file's source confirmed 18 genuine matches cleared for use with credit: Anthropic, Applied Intuition, Cohere, Cursor, Databricks, ElevenLabs, Glean, HeyGen, Lovable, Mistral AI, Notion, OpenAI, OpenEvidence, Perplexity, Physical Intelligence, Replit, Runway and Suno. Twelve cached files were confirmed mismatches and dropped — a similarly named but unrelated entity (e.g. Clay→Clay Telecom, Harvey→PJ Harvey the musician, Synthesia→the piano-learning app, World Labs→the CIA World Factbook). The remaining 32 of 50 companies (dropped + never-found) get a clean CSS typographic wordmark card instead of a fabricated logo.

caveats.content: Funding figures are cumulative capital raised, rounded by Forbes (e.g. '$60 B'), and point-in-time as of the 2025 list — several have since increased substantially.
'$0 M' for Midjourney and Surge AI denotes bootstrapped/undisclosed financing, not literally zero capital; both are treated as 0 in totals, which slightly understates true cohort capital.

The 'What It Does' categories are an analyst-imposed taxonomy over one-line editorial descriptions; a few companies could plausibly sit in two buckets (e.g. Databricks as data/analytics vs infrastructure).

This is a curated editorial list of private companies only; it omits public AI leaders and any private company Forbes' algorithm did not surface, so it is a sketch of the frontier rather than a census.
